On the Balance Sheet, Cash decreases by $100, which balances with a $100 decrease in Shareholders' Equity via Retained Earnings.
mistakes: Recording dividends as an Income Statement expense.
Treating dividends as tax-deductible.
Reducing Common Stock rather than Retained Earnings.

items.q: A company has recorded $100 in income tax expense on its Income Statement. All $100 of it is paid, in cash, in the current period. Now we change it and only $90 of it is paid in cash, with $10 being deferred to future periods. How do the statements change?
items.a: The Income Statement does not change because total tax expense remains $100, keeping Net Income the same. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is unchanged, but the $10 in deferred taxes is added back as a non-cash item, increasing ending cash by $10. On the Balance Sheet, Cash increases by $10, which balances with a $10 increase in Deferred Tax Liabilities.
rubric: The Income Statement does not change because total tax expense remains $100, keeping Net Income the same.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is unchanged, but the $10 in deferred taxes is added back as a non-cash item, increasing ending cash by $10.
On the Balance Sheet, Cash increases by $10, which balances with a $10 increase in Deferred Tax Liabilities.
mistakes: Reducing Net Income because less cash tax was paid, when total tax expense is unchanged.
Forgetting to add the deferred portion back as a non-cash item.
Recording a Deferred Tax Asset rather than a Liability - paying less cash tax now means owing more later.

items.q: Walk me through a $100 Write-Down of Debt – as in OWED Debt, a Liability – on a company’s Balance Sheet and how it affects the 3 statements.
items.a: On the Income Statement, writing down $100 of debt increases pre-tax income by $100, resulting in a $60 increase in Net Income assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $60, but we subtract the non-cash $100 write-down, causing Cash Flow from Operations and ending Cash to decrease by $40. On the Balance Sheet, Cash decreases by $40, reducing Assets by $40, while on the liabilities and equity side, Debt decreases by $100 and Shareholders' Equity increases by $60, balancing the statement with a net decrease of $40.
rubric: Recognises that writing down a liability produces a gain, raising Pre-Tax Income by $100.
States that Net Income rises by $60 at the 40% tax rate.
Subtracts the $100 non-cash gain within Cash Flow from Operations.
Concludes that ending cash falls by $40, which is the cash tax paid on a gain that brought in no cash.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Cash down $40 on the Assets side, against Debt down $100 and Shareholders' Equity up $60.
mistakes: Treating the write-down of owed debt as a loss rather than a gain.
Concluding that cash rises because Net Income rose, missing that the gain is non-cash while the tax on it is not.
Forgetting to reverse the non-cash gain on the Cash Flow Statement.

items.q: If writing down Liabilities boosts Net Income, why don’t companies just do it all the time?
items.a: While writing down liabilities provides a short-term boost to Net Income, doing so repeatedly severely damages a company's credibility with investors and lenders. In the long run, the company's inability to secure future debt or capital will harm its business far more than any temporary accounting benefit to Net Income.
rubric: While writing down liabilities provides a short-term boost to Net Income, doing so repeatedly severely damages a company's credibility with investors and lenders.
In the long run, the company's inability to secure future debt or capital will harm its business far more than any temporary accounting benefit to Net Income.
mistakes: Treating it as a purely accounting question and missing the reputational and financing consequences.
Assuming a company can simply choose to write down debt, when it requires the creditor to agree or a restructuring.
Missing that the gain is taxable, so the manoeuvre actually consumes cash.

items.q: What’s the difference between LIFO and FIFO? Can you walk me through an example of how they differ?
items.a: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) and FIFO (First-In, First-Out) are accounting methods used to value inventory and calculate Cost of Goods Sold (COGS). LIFO assumes the most recently purchased inventory items are sold first, whereas FIFO assumes the oldest inventory items are sold first. For example, in an inflationary environment where inventory costs are rising, LIFO will result in a higher COGS, lower Net Income, and lower ending inventory value compared to FIFO.
rubric: LIFO (Last-In, First-Out) and FIFO (First-In, First-Out) are accounting methods used to value inventory and calculate Cost of Goods Sold (COGS).
LIFO assumes the most recently purchased inventory items are sold first, whereas FIFO assumes the oldest inventory items are sold first.
For example, in an inflationary environment where inventory costs are rising, LIFO will result in a higher COGS, lower Net Income, and lower ending inventory value compared to FIFO.
mistakes: Reversing the two definitions.
Getting the inflation effect backwards - under LIFO, rising costs mean higher COGS and lower reported income.
Forgetting that IFRS prohibits LIFO, so the comparison only arises under US GAAP.
Missing that lower reported income under LIFO also means lower cash taxes, which is why companies choose it.

items.q: Let’s say Apple is buying $100 worth of new iPad factories with debt. How are all 3 statements affected at the start of “Year 1,” before anything else happens?
items.a: At the start of Year 1, there are no changes to the Income Statement. On the Cash Flow Statement, the $100 capital expenditure reduces Cash Flow from Investing, but this is offset by a $100 increase in Cash Flow from Financing from the debt issuance, leaving the net change in cash at zero. On the Balance Sheet, PP&E increases by $100 on the Assets side, which is balanced by a $100 increase in Debt on the Liabilities side.
rubric: At the start of Year 1, there are no changes to the Income Statement.

On the Cash Flow Statement, the $100 capital expenditure reduces Cash Flow from Investing, but this is offset by a $100 increase in Cash Flow from Financing from the debt issuance, leaving the net change in cash at zero.
On the Balance Sheet, PP&E increases by $100 on the Assets side, which is balanced by a $100 increase in Debt on the Liabilities side.
mistakes: Recording depreciation or interest before any time has passed.
Showing a net cash outflow and forgetting the offsetting debt issuance.
Expensing the factory purchase rather than capitalising it as PP&E.

items.q: Assume Apple buys $100 of factories with 10% high-yield debt. One year later, at the start of Year 2, the factories depreciate at 10% per year and no debt principal is paid off. What happens to the 3 statements, tracking only the changes after the initial purchase?
items.a: On the Income Statement, operating income decreases by $10 due to depreciation, and interest expense increases by $10, reducing pre-tax income by $20 and Net Income by $12 at a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $12, but adding back the $10 non-cash depreciation results in a net cash decrease of $2. On the Balance Sheet, Cash is down by $2 and PP&E is down by $10, reducing total Assets by $12, which matches the $12 reduction in Shareholders' Equity from the lower Net Income.
rubric: On the Income Statement, operating income decreases by $10 due to depreciation, and interest expense increases by $10, reducing pre-tax income by $20 and Net Income by $12 at a 40% tax rate.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $12, but adding back the $10 non-cash depreciation results in a net cash decrease of $2.
On the Balance Sheet, Cash is down by $2 and PP&E is down by $10, reducing total Assets by $12, which matches the $12 reduction in Shareholders' Equity from the lower Net Income.
mistakes: Forgetting the interest expense, and modelling only the depreciation.
Failing to add the depreciation back on the Cash Flow Statement.
Reducing the debt balance when the question states no principal is repaid.
Missing that cash falls by only $2 because depreciation and the tax shield offset most of the interest.

items.q: At the end of Year 2, the factories (originally worth $100, depreciated to $80) break down and their value is written down to $0, and the $100 loan must be paid back. Walk me through how the 3 statements are affected from the start of Year 2 to the end of Year 2.
items.a: On the Income Statement, the company records $10 of depreciation, an $80 write-down, and $10 of interest expense, reducing pre-tax income by $100 and Net Income by $60 at a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $60, but adding back the non-cash $10 depreciation and $80 write-down yields a positive operating cash flow of $30, which is offset by a $100 cash outflow in financing to pay back the loan, resulting in a net cash decrease of $70. On the Balance Sheet, Cash is down by $70 and PP&E is down by $90, reducing Assets by $160, which balances with the liabilities and equity side where Debt is down by $100 and Shareholders' Equity is down by $60.
rubric: Records $10 of depreciation, an $80 write-down and $10 of interest expense on the Income Statement.
States that Pre-Tax Income falls $100 and Net Income falls $60 at the 40% tax rate.
Adds back both non-cash charges, the $10 of depreciation and the $80 write-down, for $30 of operating cash flow.
Records the $100 loan repayment as a financing outflow, for a net cash decrease of $70.
States that PP&E falls by $90 over the year: $10 of depreciation and then the $80 write-down to zero.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Assets down $160 against Debt down $100 and Shareholders' Equity down $60.
mistakes: Running the loan repayment through the Income Statement rather than the financing section.
Adding back the depreciation but not the write-down, or the reverse.
Writing PP&E down by $80 only, forgetting the $10 of Year 2 depreciation that came first.
Missing that operating cash flow is positive at $30 even though Net Income is deeply negative.

items.q: Now let’s say they sell the iPads for revenue of $20, at a cost of $10. Walk me through the 3 statements under this scenario.
items.a: On the Income Statement, revenue increases by $20 and COGS increases by $10, resulting in a $10 increase in pre-tax income and a $6 increase in Net Income assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $6, and the $10 inventory reduction is added back, leading to a $16 increase in ending cash. On the Balance Sheet, cash increases by $16 and inventory decreases by $10, resulting in a net asset increase of $6, which perfectly balances with the $6 increase in Shareholders' Equity from Net Income.
rubric: On the Income Statement, revenue increases by $20 and COGS increases by $10, resulting in a $10 increase in pre-tax income and a $6 increase in Net Income assuming a 40% tax rate.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $6, and the $10 inventory reduction is added back, leading to a $16 increase in ending cash.

On the Balance Sheet, cash increases by $16 and inventory decreases by $10, resulting in a net asset increase of $6, which perfectly balances with the $6 increase in Shareholders' Equity from Net Income.
mistakes: Forgetting to add back the inventory reduction, and reporting cash up only $6.
Recognising the full $20 as profit and skipping COGS.
Reducing inventory by the $20 sale price rather than the $10 cost.

items.q: A company raises $100 worth of Debt, at 5% interest and 10% yearly principal repayment, to purchase $100 worth of Short-Term Securities with 10% interest attached. Walk me through how the 3 statements change immediately after this initial purchase.
items.a: Immediately after the purchase, there are no changes to the Income Statement. On the Cash Flow Statement, the $100 purchase of short-term securities is recorded as a cash outflow under Cash Flow from Investing, while the $100 debt raise is a cash inflow under Cash Flow from Financing, leaving ending cash unchanged. On the Balance Sheet, Short-Term Securities increase by $100 on the Assets side, and Debt increases by $100 on the Liabilities side, keeping the statement in balance.
rubric: States that there are no changes to the Income Statement at the moment of purchase.
Records the $100 purchase of short-term securities as an outflow within Cash Flow from Investing.
Records the $100 debt raise as an inflow within Cash Flow from Financing.
Concludes that ending cash is unchanged because the two offset.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Short-Term Securities up $100 on the Assets side against Debt up $100 on the Liabilities side.
mistakes: Recording interest income or interest expense before any time has passed.
Showing a cash outflow for the securities without the offsetting financing inflow.
Classifying the purchase of securities under operating rather than investing activities.

items.q: A company raises $100 of Debt at 5% interest and 10% yearly principal repayment to purchase $100 of Short-Term Securities with 10% interest. Walk me through what happens to the 3 statements at the end of Year 1, after the company has earned interest, paid interest, and paid back some of the debt principal.
items.a: On the Income Statement, the company recognizes $10 of interest income and $5 of interest expense, increasing pre-tax income by $5 and Net Income by $3 assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $3, but the company pays down $10 of debt principal under Cash Flow from Financing, resulting in a net cash decrease of $7. On the Balance Sheet, cash decreases by $7, while on the other side, debt decreases by $10 and Shareholders' Equity increases by $3 from Net Income, balancing both sides at a net decrease of $7.
rubric: On the Income Statement, the company recognizes $10 of interest income and $5 of interest expense, increasing pre-tax income by $5 and Net Income by $3 assuming a 40% tax rate.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $3, but the company pays down $10 of debt principal under Cash Flow from Financing, resulting in a net cash decrease of $7.
On the Balance Sheet, cash decreases by $7, while on the other side, debt decreases by $10 and Shareholders' Equity increases by $3 from Net Income, balancing both sides at a net decrease of $7.
mistakes: Netting interest income against interest expense and forgetting one of the two.
Running the $10 principal repayment through the Income Statement.
Concluding cash rises because Net Income rose, missing the principal repayment.
Calculating the principal repayment off the remaining balance rather than the original $100.

items.q: A company holds $100 of Short-Term Securities and $90 of remaining Debt from a prior transaction. At the end of Year 1, the company sells the $100 of Short-Term Securities for $110 and uses the proceeds to repay the $90 of remaining Debt. Walk me through the 3 statements after only these changes.
items.a: On the Income Statement, a $10 gain is recorded, increasing pre-tax income by $10 and Net Income by $6 assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $6, but the $10 non-cash gain is subtracted, while the $110 sale proceeds are added under Cash Flow from Investing, and the $90 debt repayment is subtracted under Cash Flow from Financing, resulting in a net cash increase of $16. On the Balance Sheet, cash increases by $16 and short-term securities decrease by $100, resulting in a net asset decrease of $84, which balances with the liabilities side where debt decreases by $90 and Shareholders' Equity increases by $6.
rubric: Records a $10 gain, being $110 of proceeds against the $100 carrying value.
States that Pre-Tax Income rises $10 and Net Income rises $6 at the 40% tax rate.
Subtracts the $10 non-cash gain within Cash Flow from Operations.
Adds the full $110 of sale proceeds within Cash Flow from Investing.
Subtracts the $90 debt repayment within Cash Flow from Financing.
Arrives at a net cash increase of $16.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Cash up $16 and Short-Term Securities down $100, against Debt down $90 and Shareholders' Equity up $6.
mistakes: Recording only the $10 gain in investing rather than the full $110 of proceeds.
Failing to reverse the non-cash gain, double-counting it against the proceeds.
Running the $90 debt repayment through the Income Statement.
Forgetting the tax on the gain, and answering that cash rises by $20.

items.q: Explain what a Deferred Tax Asset or Deferred Tax Liability is. How do they usually get created?
items.a: A Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) represents cash taxes that a company will owe in the future due to underpaying taxes in the current period, while a Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) represents future tax savings from overpaying taxes previously. Both arise from temporary timing differences between book accounting and tax accounting. They are most commonly created through differences in depreciation methods, asset write-ups in M&A transactions, or differing treatments of pension contributions.
rubric: Defines a Deferred Tax Liability as cash taxes owed in future because the company underpaid cash tax relative to book tax in the current period.
Defines a Deferred Tax Asset as future tax savings arising because the company overpaid cash tax relative to book tax.
States that both arise from temporary timing differences between book and tax accounting, not permanent ones.
Names common causes: different depreciation methods for book and tax, asset write-ups in M&A, and differing treatment of pension contributions.
mistakes: Reversing the two, so a DTL is described as a future saving.
Attributing deferred taxes to permanent differences, which never create one.
Failing to name a concrete cause such as accelerated tax depreciation or an M&A write-up.

items.q: How can both Deferred Tax Assets (DTAs) and Deferred Tax Liabilities (DTLs) exist at the same time on a company's Balance Sheet?
items.a: Both DTAs and DTLs can coexist because they are created by different underlying transactions and events. For example, a company might have Net Operating Losses (NOLs) from early unprofitable years that create a Deferred Tax Asset. At the same time, the company might use accelerated depreciation for tax purposes and straight-line depreciation for book purposes, which generates a Deferred Tax Liability.
rubric: Both DTAs and DTLs can coexist because they are created by different underlying transactions and events.
For example, a company might have Net Operating Losses (NOLs) from early unprofitable years that create a Deferred Tax Asset.
At the same time, the company might use accelerated depreciation for tax purposes and straight-line depreciation for book purposes, which generates a Deferred Tax Liability.
mistakes: Assuming a company nets its DTAs and DTLs to a single balance, when they are separately disclosed and only offset within the same tax jurisdiction.
Believing one must cancel the other out because they point in opposite directions.
Failing to give two distinct causes, which is what the question is actually asking for.

items.q: How do Income Taxes Payable and Income Taxes Receivable differ from DTLs and DTAs? Aren’t they the same concept?
items.a: Although similar, they are distinct concepts. Income Taxes Payable and Receivable are short-term accrual accounts representing taxes owed or owed back for the current fiscal year. In contrast, Deferred Tax Assets (DTAs) and Deferred Tax Liabilities (DTLs) are typically longer-term balance sheet items that arise from temporary timing differences between book and tax accounting, often triggered by non-operating events.
rubric: States that the two are related but distinct.
Describes Income Taxes Payable and Receivable as short-term accrual accounts for taxes owed, or owed back, for the current fiscal year.
Describes DTAs and DTLs as longer-term items arising from temporary timing differences between book and tax accounting.
Notes that deferred items are often triggered by non-operating events such as an acquisition, where the payable and receivable arise from the ordinary annual tax computation.
mistakes: Treating Income Taxes Payable as a deferred tax item because both concern taxes not yet paid in cash.
Missing the timing distinction: the payable settles within the year, the deferred item reverses over years.
Failing to note that deferred items are created by book-versus-tax differences rather than by the timing of the cash payment.

items.q: How do you project Balance Sheet items like Accounts Receivable and Accrued Expenses over several years in a 3-statement model?
items.a: These items are typically projected as a percentage of their corresponding Income Statement drivers. For instance, Accounts Receivable and Deferred Revenue are tied to Revenue, Inventory is tied to COGS, and Accrued Expenses, Prepaid Expenses, and Accounts Payable are tied to Operating Expenses. Alternatively, you can project these items using working capital ratios like "days outstanding" (e.g., Accounts Receivable Days), assuming the days collection period remains constant and calculating the balance sheet metric from there.
rubric: States that these items are normally projected as a percentage of their corresponding Income Statement driver.
Ties Accounts Receivable and Deferred Revenue to Revenue.
Ties Inventory to COGS.
Ties Accrued Expenses, Prepaid Expenses and Accounts Payable to Operating Expenses.
Gives the alternative of working capital ratios such as Accounts Receivable Days, holding the days constant and backing the balance out from it.
mistakes: Tying Inventory or Accounts Payable to Revenue rather than to COGS or Operating Expenses.
Growing balance sheet items at a flat percentage with no link to any driver.
Holding a days ratio constant when the business model is changing, which is exactly when it will not hold.

items.q: How should you project Depreciation and Capital Expenditures?
items.a: There are three main approaches to projecting Depreciation and Capital Expenditures. The simplest method is to project both as a percentage of revenue. Alternatively, you can make Depreciation a percentage of revenue while projecting CapEx as a historical average, a constant dollar increase, or a fixed percentage growth rate. The most complex method involves building a detailed PP&E schedule that estimates CapEx based on management's expansion plans and depreciates both existing and new assets using their useful lives and the straight-line method.
rubric: States that there are three approaches, ranging from simple to detailed.
Gives the simplest: project both Depreciation and CapEx as a percentage of revenue.
Gives the middle approach: Depreciation as a percentage of revenue, with CapEx from a historical average, a constant dollar increase, or a fixed growth rate.
Gives the most detailed: a full PP&E schedule with CapEx driven by management's expansion plans.
States that in the detailed schedule both existing and newly added assets are depreciated over their useful lives, normally straight-line.
mistakes: Setting Depreciation equal to CapEx in every year, which assumes a steady state the company may not be in.
Letting CapEx fall below Depreciation indefinitely for a growing company.
Forgetting to depreciate newly added assets in the detailed schedule.

items.q: Let’s take a step back… there’s usually a “simple” and “complex” way of projecting a company’s financial statements. Is there a real advantage to using the complex method? In other words, does it give us better numbers?
items.a: No, complex methods do not necessarily yield more accurate numbers, as the final outputs are often very similar to simpler methods. Instead, the primary advantage of a complex model is that it provides better support and justification for your assumptions. For example, rather than assuming an arbitrary revenue growth rate, a bottom-up model allows you to attribute that growth to specific drivers like price increases, volume growth, or geographic expansion.
rubric: No, complex methods do not necessarily yield more accurate numbers, as the final outputs are often very similar to simpler methods.
Instead, the primary advantage of a complex model is that it provides better support and justification for your assumptions.

For example, rather than assuming an arbitrary revenue growth rate, a bottom-up model allows you to attribute that growth to specific drivers like price increases, volume growth, or geographic expansion.
mistakes: Claiming the complex model produces materially more accurate outputs.
Concluding the complex model is therefore pointless, missing that defensibility is the actual benefit.
Failing to give an example of what a detailed build lets you attribute growth to.

items.q: What are examples of non-recurring charges we need to add back to a company’s EBIT / EBITDA when analyzing its financial statements?
items.a: Common non-recurring charges to add back include restructuring charges, goodwill impairment, asset write-downs, bad debt expenses, one-time legal fees, disaster expenses, and changes in accounting policies. To qualify as an add-back for EBIT or EBITDA, these charges must impact operating income on the Income Statement; "below the line" items are excluded. Note that standard non-cash charges like depreciation and amortization are added back but are not considered non-recurring since they occur every year.
rubric: Common non-recurring charges to add back include restructuring charges, goodwill impairment, asset write-downs, bad debt expenses, one-time legal fees, disaster expenses, and changes in accounting policies.
To qualify as an add-back for EBIT or EBITDA, these charges must impact operating income on the Income Statement; "below the line" items are excluded.
Note that standard non-cash charges like depreciation and amortization are added back but are not considered non-recurring since they occur every year.
mistakes: Adding back a charge that sits below the operating line, which never touched EBIT in the first place.
Treating depreciation and amortisation as non-recurring rather than simply non-cash.
Adding back restructuring charges that recur every single year, which makes them ordinary operating cost.
Forgetting to check whether the add-back is tax-affected when comparing to a peer's adjusted figure.

items.q: What’s the difference between capital leases and operating leases? How do they affect the statements?
items.a:
Under the current standards - ASC 842 in US GAAP and IFRS 16 - every lease longer than 12 months goes on the Balance Sheet as a Right-of-Use Asset with a matching Lease Liability. The old off-balance-sheet operating lease is gone, and 'capital lease' is now called 'finance lease'.

What still differs is the Income Statement.

US GAAP keeps two classes. An OPERATING lease produces a single straight-line lease expense inside Operating Income, and the whole cash payment sits in CFO. A FINANCE lease is split into Amortisation of the ROU Asset plus Interest on the liability, so total expense is front-loaded, and the principal portion of the payment moves to CFF.

IFRS 16 has no operating-lease class for a lessee - every lease is treated the finance-lease way.

Classification under ASC 842 turns on whether the lease effectively transfers control: ownership transfers at the end, a purchase option reasonably certain to be exercised, a term covering a major part of the asset's economic life, a present value of payments amounting to substantially all of fair value, or an asset so specialised it has no alternative use. The old 75%-of-life and 90%-of-fair-value bright lines were removed as tests, though they survive in practice as rules of thumb for 'major part' and 'substantially all'.

The consequence for valuation: an IFRS company's EBITDA excludes its entire lease cost while a US GAAP company's EBITDA is still charged for its operating leases, which is why you add operating lease liabilities to Enterprise Value under IFRS but not under US GAAP.
rubric: States that under ASC 842 and IFRS 16, every lease longer than 12 months goes on the Balance Sheet as a Right-of-Use Asset with a matching Lease Liability.
Notes that the off-balance-sheet operating lease is gone, and that a capital lease is now called a finance lease.
States that under US GAAP an operating lease produces a single straight-line lease expense inside Operating Income, with the whole cash payment in CFO.
States that a finance lease splits into Amortisation of the ROU Asset plus Interest, front-loading total expense and moving the principal portion of the payment to CFF.
States that IFRS 16 has no lessee operating-lease class, so every lease gets the finance-lease treatment.

Gives the ASC 842 classification tests as control-transfer indicators: ownership transfer, a purchase option reasonably certain of exercise, a term covering a major part of economic life, present value amounting to substantially all of fair value, or a specialised asset with no alternative use.
Notes that the old 75%-of-life and 90%-of-fair-value bright lines were removed as tests and survive only as rules of thumb.
Explains the valuation consequence: an IFRS filer's EBITDA excludes the whole lease cost, so operating lease liabilities are added to Enterprise Value under IFRS but not under US GAAP.
mistakes: Describing operating leases as off-balance-sheet, which has not been true since ASC 842 and IFRS 16 took effect.
Quoting the 75%-of-useful-life or 90%-of-fair-value bright lines as the current classification tests.
Applying the US GAAP operating-lease treatment to an IFRS filer, which has no such lessee class.
Comparing EBITDA across an IFRS filer and a US GAAP filer without adjusting for the lease treatment.

items.q: How do Net Operating Losses (NOLs) affect a company’s 3 statements?
items.a: In a simple approach, you reduce taxable income by the portion of NOLs utilized during the year, calculate the new tax expense, and subtract this from pre-tax income while reducing the Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) balance by the amount used. A more complex approach involves creating a book-versus-cash tax schedule to calculate taxable income with NOLs and comparing it to taxes without NOLs. The difference is then recorded as an increase to the Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) on the Balance Sheet, which reflects the cash savings while keeping book and cash taxes separate.
rubric: Simple approach: reduce taxable income by the NOLs used in the year and compute the lower tax expense on that base.
Simple approach: subtract that tax expense from pre-tax income and reduce the Deferred Tax Asset balance by the amount of NOL consumed.
Complex approach: build a book-versus-cash tax schedule, computing taxable income with the NOLs applied and comparing it against taxes without them.
States that the difference between book and cash taxes is recorded as an increase to the Deferred Tax Liability.
Explains that this keeps book and cash taxes separate while still reflecting the cash saving.
mistakes: Under the complex, book-versus-cash approach, reducing book tax expense as well as cash tax - there the NOL saves cash tax and the gap goes to deferred taxes.
Forgetting to draw down the Deferred Tax Asset as the NOL is consumed.
Treating the NOL benefit as a permanent difference, when it is a timing difference that reverses as the balance is used.

Mixing the two approaches: the simple one runs the benefit through book tax expense and draws down the DTA, the complex one keeps book tax at the statutory rate and puts the difference in deferred taxes. Pick one and stay in it.

items.q: Let’s say you’re creating quarterly projections for a company rather than annual projections. What’s the best way to project revenue growth each quarter?
items.a: The best approach is to analyze historical quarterly data and project growth on a Year-over-Year (YoY) basis for each specific quarter. Comparing quarters sequentially (Quarter-over-Quarter) is generally ineffective because many businesses experience significant seasonality. Applying YoY growth rates ensures that seasonal fluctuations in both revenue and expenses are properly accounted for in the quarterly model.
rubric: The best approach is to analyze historical quarterly data and project growth on a Year-over-Year (YoY) basis for each specific quarter.
Comparing quarters sequentially (Quarter-over-Quarter) is generally ineffective because many businesses experience significant seasonality.
Applying YoY growth rates ensures that seasonal fluctuations in both revenue and expenses are properly accounted for in the quarterly model.
mistakes: Projecting quarter-over-quarter growth and mistaking seasonality for a trend.
Applying one annual growth rate evenly across four quarters.
Applying the year-over-year approach to revenue but not to the expense lines, so margins distort.

items.q: What happens to the Deferred Tax Asset / Deferred Tax Liability line item if we record accelerated Depreciation for tax purposes, but straight-line Depreciation for book purposes?
items.a: Using accelerated depreciation for tax purposes and straight-line depreciation for book purposes creates a temporary timing difference. In the early years, tax depreciation is higher, which reduces cash taxes paid and causes the Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) on the Balance Sheet to increase. In later years, this trend reverses as tax depreciation falls below book depreciation, causing the company to pay higher cash taxes and gradually reduce the DTL balance to zero.
rubric: Using accelerated depreciation for tax purposes and straight-line depreciation for book purposes creates a temporary timing difference.
In the early years, tax depreciation is higher, which reduces cash taxes paid and causes the Deferred Tax Liability (DTL) on the Balance Sheet to increase.
In later years, this trend reverses as tax depreciation falls below book depreciation, causing the company to pay higher cash taxes and gradually reduce the DTL balance to zero.
mistakes: Creating a Deferred Tax Asset instead of a Liability - paying less cash tax now means owing more later.
Treating the difference as permanent rather than as a timing difference that reverses.
Forgetting that total depreciation over the asset's life is identical under both methods.

items.q: If you own over 50% but less than 100% of another company, what happens on the financial statements when you record the acquisition?
items.a: When you acquire a majority stake between 50% and 100% of another company, you must consolidate the financial statements. This means you add 100% of the target company's assets, liabilities, revenues, and expenses to your own financial statements. To account for the portion of the company you do not own, you create a "Noncontrolling Interest" (or Minority Interest) line item on the Balance Sheet and Income Statement to reflect the minority shareholders' share of net assets and net income.
rubric: States that a stake above 50% requires full consolidation.
States that you add 100% of the target's assets, liabilities, revenues and expenses, not your ownership percentage.
Creates a Noncontrolling Interest line on the Balance Sheet for the minority shareholders' share of net assets.
Creates a corresponding Noncontrolling Interest deduction on the Income Statement for the minority's share of net income.
Explains that this is what reconciles 100% consolidation with less than 100% ownership.
mistakes: Consolidating only the owned percentage of the target's assets and revenue instead of 100%.
Using the equity method, which applies below the control threshold rather than above it.
Omitting the Noncontrolling Interest, so the Balance Sheet claims the minority's share belongs to the parent's shareholders.
Forgetting the Income Statement deduction and overstating Net Income to Common.

items.q: What about if you own between 20% and 50% of another company? How do you record this acquisition and how are the statements affected?
items.a: When you own between 20% and 50% of a company, you record it as an Equity Interest (or Associate Company) and do not consolidate the financial statements. Instead, you record your share of the company's value as an asset called "Investments in Equity Interests" on the Balance Sheet. On the Income Statement, you add your share of the company's Net Income, which is then subtracted on the Cash Flow Statement as a non-cash adjustment. Over time, the asset increases by your share of Net Income and decreases by any dividends received.
rubric: When you own between 20% and 50% of a company, you record it as an Equity Interest (or Associate Company) and do not consolidate the financial statements.
Instead, you record your share of the company's value as an asset called "Investments in Equity Interests" on the Balance Sheet.
On the Income Statement, you add your share of the company's Net Income, which is then subtracted on the Cash Flow Statement as a non-cash adjustment.
Over time, the asset increases by your share of Net Income and decreases by any dividends received.
mistakes: Consolidating the associate's revenue and expenses, which only applies above 50%.
Forgetting to reverse the equity-method income as a non-cash item on the Cash Flow Statement.
Failing to reduce the investment balance when dividends are received.
Recording 100% of the associate's net income rather than the ownership share.

items.q: What if you own less than 20% of another company?
items.a: If you own less than 20% of a company, accounting treatments can vary. If you exert "significant influence," you may still use the Equity Interest method. Otherwise, you classify the holding as a simple Investment or Security on the Balance Sheet, ignoring the other company's overall financials and only recording dividends or changes in the security's value.
rubric: If you own less than 20% of a company, accounting treatments can vary.
If you exert "significant influence," you may still use the Equity Interest method.

Otherwise, you classify the holding as a simple Investment or Security on the Balance Sheet, ignoring the other company's overall financials and only recording dividends or changes in the security's value.
mistakes: Treating the 20% line as absolute, when significant influence is the actual test.
Applying the equity method to a passive holding with no influence.
Recording a share of the investee's net income under the security treatment.

items.q: What are the different classifications for Securities that a company can use on its Balance Sheet? How do they differ?
items.a: Securities on a Balance Sheet are classified into three categories: Trading, Available for Sale (AFS), and Held-to-Maturity (HTM). Trading securities are short-term investments where all realized and unrealized gains and losses are recognized on the Income Statement. AFS securities are longer-term, marked to market on the Balance Sheet, with unrealized gains and losses recorded in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI). HTM securities are long-term holdings where unrealized gains and losses are not recorded, and changes are only recognized upon actual sale.
rubric: Securities on a Balance Sheet are classified into three categories: Trading, Available for Sale (AFS), and Held-to-Maturity (HTM).
Trading securities are short-term investments where all realized and unrealized gains and losses are recognized on the Income Statement.
AFS securities are longer-term, marked to market on the Balance Sheet, with unrealized gains and losses recorded in Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI).
HTM securities are long-term holdings where unrealized gains and losses are not recorded, and changes are only recognized upon actual sale.
mistakes: Routing AFS unrealised gains through the Income Statement rather than through AOCI.
Marking Held-to-Maturity securities to market, when they are carried at amortised cost.
Forgetting that under current US GAAP this three-way split applies to debt securities, while equity securities are generally carried at fair value through net income.
Confusing realised gains, which always hit the Income Statement, with unrealised ones.

items.q: Now let’s take the opposite scenario and say that you own 30% of another company. The other company earns Net Income of $20. Walk me through the 3 statements after you record the portion of Net Income that’s you’re entitled to.
items.a: On the Income Statement, you record $6 (30% of the $20 Net Income) as "Net Income from Equity Interests," which increases your Net Income by $6. On the Cash Flow Statement, you start with the $6 increase in Net Income but subtract it as a non-cash adjustment because you have not actually received this cash, leaving ending cash unchanged. On the Balance Sheet, the "Investments in Equity Interests" asset increases by $6, which is balanced by a $6 increase in Retained Earnings under Shareholders' Equity.
rubric: On the Income Statement, you record $6 (30% of the $20 Net Income) as "Net Income from Equity Interests," which increases your Net Income by $6.
On the Cash Flow Statement, you start with the $6 increase in Net Income but subtract it as a non-cash adjustment because you have not actually received this cash, leaving ending cash unchanged.
On the Balance Sheet, the "Investments in Equity Interests" asset increases by $6, which is balanced by a $6 increase in Retained Earnings under Shareholders' Equity.
mistakes: Consolidating 30% of the associate's revenue and expenses instead of recording the share of net income.
Forgetting to reverse the $6 as a non-cash item, and concluding cash rises.
Recording the full $20 of the associate's net income rather than the 30% share.

items.q: Now let’s assume that this 30% owned company issues Dividends of $10. Taking into account the changes from the last question, walk me through the 3 statements again and explain what’s different now.
items.a:
The Income Statement is unchanged: Net Income is still up by $6 from your 30% share of the associate's $20 of Net Income. A dividend received from an associate is not income - you already recognised the earnings.

Cash Flow Statement: start with Net Income up $6, subtract the $6 of equity-method income as a non-cash item, then add the $3 dividend actually received (30% of $10) in Cash Flow from Operations. Cash is up by $3.

Balance Sheet: Cash is up by $3. Investments in Equity Interests moves +$6 for your share of Net Income and -$3 for the dividend, so that line is up by $3 NET. Total Assets are therefore up by $6 ($3 of cash plus $3 on the investment line), which balances the $6 increase in Retained Earnings.

Intuition: the dividend converts part of the investment balance into cash. It does not change total assets or equity - it changes the form the asset takes.
rubric: States that the Income Statement is unchanged, with Net Income still up $6 from the 30% share of the associate's $20 of Net Income.
Explains that a dividend received from an associate is not income, because the earnings were already recognised.
On the Cash Flow Statement, starts from Net Income up $6, subtracts the $6 of equity-method income as non-cash, and adds the $3 dividend actually received.
Concludes that cash is up $3.
States that Investments in Equity Interests moves +$6 for the share of net income and -$3 for the dividend, so that line is up $3 NET.
States that Total Assets are up $6 - $3 of cash plus $3 on the investment line - balancing the $6 increase in Retained Earnings.
Explains that the dividend converts part of the investment balance into cash without changing total assets or equity.
mistakes: Recording the $3 dividend as income, double-counting the associate's earnings.
Failing to reverse the $6 of equity-method income as a non-cash item on the Cash Flow Statement.
Leaving the investment line up $6 rather than $3 net after the dividend.
Consolidating 30% of the associate's revenue and expenses instead of using the equity method.

items.q: If a company holds only a 10% stake in another company (not a controlling or significant-influence stake), how is that investment treated on the financial statements?
items.a:
A 10% stake is below the 20% threshold, so it is normally treated as a security or short-term investment rather than through the equity method. Under that treatment you record only the dividends received, plus any change in the security's fair value depending on its classification, and you ignore the other company's net income entirely.

The threshold is a presumption rather than a hard rule, though. If you can demonstrate "significant influence" over the 10%-owned company - a board seat, say, or material involvement in its operating policy - the equity method applies despite the small stake.
rubric: States that a 10% stake sits below the 20% threshold, so it is normally treated as a security or short-term investment.
States that under that treatment you record only dividends received, and any change in the security's value, ignoring the investee's net income.
Explains that the 20% line is a presumption about significant influence rather than a hard rule.
States that with demonstrable significant influence - a board seat, involvement in operating policy - the equity method applies even below 20%.
mistakes: Applying the equity method automatically to any minority stake.
Recording 10% of the investee's net income, which is the equity method rather than the security treatment.
Treating the 20% threshold as an absolute rule rather than a rebuttable presumption about influence.

items.q: Walk me through what happens when you pay $20 in interest on Debt, with $10 in the form of cash interest and $10 in the form of Paid-in-Kind (PIK) interest.
items.a: On the Income Statement, the entire $20 interest expense reduces Pre-Tax Income, which decreases Net Income by $12 assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $12, but you add back the $10 of non-cash PIK interest, resulting in a net cash decrease of $2. On the Balance Sheet, Cash decreases by $2 on the Assets side, while on the Liabilities and Equity side, Debt increases by $10 due to the accrued PIK interest and Retained Earnings decreases by $12, keeping the statement in balance.
rubric: States that the full $20 of interest hits the Income Statement, cash and PIK alike.
States that Net Income falls $12 at the 40% tax rate.
Adds back the $10 of non-cash PIK interest on the Cash Flow Statement.
Arrives at a net cash decrease of $2, being the $10 cash interest less the $8 tax saving on the full $20.
States that Debt increases by $10 as the PIK interest accrues onto the principal.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Cash down $2 against Debt up $10 and Retained Earnings down $12.
mistakes: Excluding the PIK interest from the Income Statement because no cash moves - it is still an expense and still tax-deductible.
Forgetting that PIK interest accrues onto the debt balance.
Adding back the PIK on the Cash Flow Statement but not increasing debt on the Balance Sheet, so it fails to balance.
Answering that cash falls by $10, ignoring the tax shield on the full $20.

items.q: A company records Book Depreciation of $10 per year for 3 years. On its Tax financial statements, it records Depreciation of $15 in year 1, $10 in year 2, and $5 in year 3. Walk me through what happens on the BOOK financial statements in Year 1.
items.a: On the Income Statement, Pre-Tax Income falls by $10 and Net Income decreases by $6 assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $6, but you add back the $10 of Depreciation and $2 of Deferred Taxes to reflect that cash taxes were lower than book taxes, resulting in a net cash increase of $6. On the Balance Sheet, Cash is up by $6 and PP&E is down by $10, reducing Assets by $4. This is balanced on the other side by a $2 increase in Deferred Tax Liabilities and a $6 decrease in Retained Earnings.
rubric: On the Income Statement, Pre-Tax Income falls by $10 and Net Income decreases by $6 assuming a 40% tax rate.

On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $6, but you add back the $10 of Depreciation and $2 of Deferred Taxes to reflect that cash taxes were lower than book taxes, resulting in a net cash increase of $6.
On the Balance Sheet, Cash is up by $6 and PP&E is down by $10, reducing Assets by $4.
This is balanced on the other side by a $2 increase in Deferred Tax Liabilities and a $6 decrease in Retained Earnings.
mistakes: Using the tax depreciation figure of $15 on the book Income Statement.
Forgetting the deferred tax adjustment, and concluding cash rises by only $4.
Creating a Deferred Tax Asset rather than a Liability - lower cash tax now means more tax owed later.
Missing that book and tax depreciation total the same $30 across the three years.

items.q: A company you’re analyzing records a Goodwill Impairment of $100. However, this Goodwill Impairment is NOT deductible for cash tax purposes. Walk me through how the 3 statements change.
items.a:
On the Income Statement, Pre-Tax Income falls by $100. Because the impairment is not deductible for cash tax purposes, it is a permanent difference: it is added back in computing taxable income, so the tax provision does not change and there is no tax shield. Net Income therefore falls by the full $100, not $60.

On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down $100 and you add back the $100 non-cash impairment, so cash is unchanged. No deferred tax adjustment is needed, because a permanent difference never creates one.

On the Balance Sheet, Goodwill is down $100 on the Assets side, and Retained Earnings is down $100 on the Liabilities and Equity side. The statement balances.

The trap: a temporary difference (book and tax eventually agree, timing differs) moves deferred taxes; a permanent difference (book and tax never agree) does not. Non-deductible goodwill impairment is permanent.
rubric: States that Pre-Tax Income falls by $100 on the Income Statement.
Identifies the non-deductible impairment as a permanent difference, so the tax provision does not change and there is no tax shield.
States that Net Income therefore falls by the full $100, not by a tax-affected amount.
States that on the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down $100 and the $100 non-cash impairment is added back, leaving cash unchanged.
States that no deferred tax adjustment is needed, because a permanent difference never creates one.
States that on the Balance Sheet, Goodwill falls $100 on the Assets side and Retained Earnings falls $100 on the Liabilities and Equity side, so it balances.
mistakes: Tax-affecting the impairment and answering that Net Income falls by $60 or $75, which is the treatment for a deductible charge.
Recording a deferred tax adjustment on the Cash Flow Statement or a change in Deferred Tax Liabilities on the Balance Sheet, which only happens for a temporary difference.
Confusing a permanent difference (book and tax never agree) with a temporary one (book and tax agree eventually, timing differs).
Forgetting to add back the impairment as a non-cash charge, and concluding that cash falls.

items.q: How can you tell whether or not a Goodwill Impairment will be tax-deductible?
items.a: It depends on how the deal was structured for tax purposes. In a stock purchase, the target's historical tax basis carries over, so the Goodwill created for book purposes has no corresponding tax basis and is not deductible. In an asset purchase (or a stock deal with a Section 338(h)(10) or 336(e) election), the buyer gets a stepped-up tax basis in the acquired assets, including Goodwill, which becomes tax-deductible and amortizable, typically over 15 years. So Goodwill from a stock deal is usually non-deductible, while Goodwill from an asset deal usually is.
rubric: States that deductibility turns on how the deal was structured for tax purposes.
States that in a stock purchase the target's historical tax basis carries over, so book Goodwill has no tax basis and is not deductible.
States that in an asset purchase the buyer takes a stepped-up tax basis in the acquired assets, including Goodwill.
Names the election that gives a stock deal asset-deal tax treatment: Section 338(h)(10) or 336(e).
States that deductible Goodwill is amortised for tax purposes, typically over 15 years.
Summarises: Goodwill from a stock deal is usually non-deductible, Goodwill from an asset deal usually is.
mistakes: Stating flatly that goodwill impairment is never tax-deductible, without reference to the deal structure.
Confusing the book treatment (impairment testing, no amortisation) with the tax treatment (15-year amortisation where a basis exists).
Forgetting the 338(h)(10) election, which is what lets a stock purchase be taxed as an asset purchase.
Assuming the buyer can choose the treatment after closing rather than at structuring.

items.q: A company has Net Operating Losses (NOLs) of $100 included in the Deferred Tax Asset (DTA) line item on its Balance Sheet because it has been unprofitable up until this point. Now, the company finally turns a profit and has Pre-Tax Income of $200 this year. Walk me through the 3 statements and assume that the NOLs can be used as a direct tax deduction on the financial statements.
items.a: On the Income Statement, applying the $100 NOL reduces Pre-Tax Income by $100, causing Net Income to fall by $60 at a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $60, but you add back the $100 non-cash NOL usage under Deferred Taxes, resulting in a net cash increase of $40. On the Balance Sheet, Cash is up by $40 and the Deferred Tax Asset decreases by $100, reducing Assets by $60, which balances with the $60 decrease in Retained Earnings.
rubric: On the Income Statement, applying the $100 NOL reduces Pre-Tax Income by $100, causing Net Income to fall by $60 at a 40% tax rate.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down by $60, but you add back the $100 non-cash NOL usage under Deferred Taxes, resulting in a net cash increase of $40.
On the Balance Sheet, Cash is up by $40 and the Deferred Tax Asset decreases by $100, reducing Assets by $60, which balances with the $60 decrease in Retained Earnings.
mistakes: Forgetting to draw down the Deferred Tax Asset as the NOL is consumed.
Treating the NOL usage as a cash outflow rather than a non-cash deferred tax movement.
Applying the full $200 of pre-tax income against a $100 NOL balance.
Missing that cash actually rises, because the NOL shelters tax that would otherwise have been paid.

items.q: You’re analyzing a company’s financial statements and you need to calendarize the revenue, EBITDA, and other items. The company has earned revenue of $1000 and EBITDA of $200 from January 1 to December 31, 2050. From January 1 to March 31, 2050, it earned revenue of $200 and EBITDA of $50. From January 1 to March 31, 2051, it earned revenue of $300 and EBITDA of $75. What are the company’s revenue and EBITDA for the Trailing Twelve Months as of March 31, 2051?
items.a: To calculate the Trailing Twelve Months (TTM) figures, you add the new partial period to the full-year period and subtract the old partial period. Using this formula, TTM Revenue is $1,100 ($300 + $1,000 - $200) and TTM EBITDA is $225 ($75 + $200 - $50).
rubric: To calculate the Trailing Twelve Months (TTM) figures, you add the new partial period to the full-year period and subtract the old partial period.
Using this formula, TTM Revenue is $1,100 ($300 + $1,000 - $200) and TTM EBITDA is $225 ($75 + $200 - $50).
mistakes: Adding the new stub period to the full year without subtracting the corresponding prior-year stub.
Subtracting the wrong stub - the one to remove is the same quarter of the earlier year.
Calendarising revenue but not EBITDA, so the implied margin is wrong.

items.q: You’re analyzing a company with $100 in Short-Term Investments on its Balance Sheet. These Investments are classified as Available-for-Sale (AFS) Securities. The market value for these securities increases to $110. Walk me through what happens on the 3 statements.
items.a: On the Income Statement, there are no changes because unrealized gains and losses on Available-for-Sale (AFS) securities are not reported here. On the Cash Flow Statement, there are also no changes because no cash has been exchanged. On the Balance Sheet, Short-Term Investments increases by $10 on the Assets side, and Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) increases by $10 under Shareholders' Equity, keeping the statement in balance.
rubric: On the Income Statement, there are no changes because unrealized gains and losses on Available-for-Sale (AFS) securities are not reported here.
On the Cash Flow Statement, there are also no changes because no cash has been exchanged.

On the Balance Sheet, Short-Term Investments increases by $10 on the Assets side, and Accumulated Other Comprehensive Income (AOCI) increases by $10 under Shareholders' Equity, keeping the statement in balance.
mistakes: Running the unrealised AFS gain through the Income Statement, which is the Trading treatment.
Recording a cash movement when no security has been sold.
Booking the gain to Retained Earnings rather than to AOCI.
Forgetting that the gain does move to the Income Statement once the security is actually sold.

items.q: A company has $100 in Short-Term Investments classified as Trading Securities. The market value of these securities increases to $110. Walk me through what happens on the 3 statements.
items.a: On the Income Statement, Pre-Tax Income increases by the $10 unrealized gain, leading to a $6 increase in Net Income assuming a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $6, but we subtract the $10 non-cash gain, resulting in a net cash decrease of $4. On the Balance Sheet, Cash is down by $4 and Short-Term Investments is up by $10, making total Assets up by $6, which balances with Shareholders' Equity (Retained Earnings) being up by $6.
rubric: On the Income Statement, Pre-Tax Income increases by the $10 unrealized gain, leading to a $6 increase in Net Income assuming a 40% tax rate.
On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is up by $6, but we subtract the $10 non-cash gain, resulting in a net cash decrease of $4.
On the Balance Sheet, Cash is down by $4 and Short-Term Investments is up by $10, making total Assets up by $6, which balances with Shareholders' Equity (Retained Earnings) being up by $6.
mistakes: Applying the AFS treatment and routing the gain through AOCI instead of the Income Statement.
Forgetting to reverse the unrealised gain as a non-cash item on the Cash Flow Statement.
Concluding cash is unchanged, and missing the tax paid on a gain that produced no cash.

items.q: Can you walk me through how to calculate EBIT and EBITDA? How are they different?
items.a: EBIT is a company's Operating Income from the Income Statement, which includes COGS, operating expenses, and non-cash charges like Depreciation & Amortization (D&A), thereby indirectly reflecting capital expenditures. EBITDA is calculated by taking EBIT and adding back Depreciation and Amortization. While EBITDA is often used as a proxy for cash flow because it excludes non-cash expenses, it differs from EBIT by completely ignoring capital expenditures.
rubric: EBIT is a company's Operating Income from the Income Statement, which includes COGS, operating expenses, and non-cash charges like Depreciation & Amortization (D&A), thereby indirectly reflecting capital expenditures.
EBITDA is calculated by taking EBIT and adding back Depreciation and Amortization.
While EBITDA is often used as a proxy for cash flow because it excludes non-cash expenses, it differs from EBIT by completely ignoring capital expenditures.
mistakes: Starting EBIT from Net Income rather than Operating Income.
Sourcing D&A from the Income Statement, where it is often partly embedded in COGS and operating expenses.
Treating EBITDA as equivalent to cash flow.
Forgetting to adjust Operating Income for non-recurring charges before calling it EBIT.

items.q: You’re analyzing the financial statements of a Public Comp, and you see Income Statement line items for Restructuring Expenses and an Asset Disposal. Should you add these back when calculating EBITDA?
items.a: First, you should verify these charges on the Cash Flow Statement or in the financial footnotes, as they may be partially embedded in other Income Statement line items. Second, you only add them back if they are truly non-recurring; if the company has restructuring expenses every year, they should be treated as recurring. Ultimately, there is no single correct way, and adjustments require careful discretion based on the persistence of the charges.
rubric: First, you should verify these charges on the Cash Flow Statement or in the financial footnotes, as they may be partially embedded in other Income Statement line items.
Second, you only add them back if they are truly non-recurring; if the company has restructuring expenses every year, they should be treated as recurring.
Ultimately, there is no single correct way, and adjustments require careful discretion based on the persistence of the charges.
mistakes: Adding back every charge labelled non-recurring without testing whether it recurs.
Adding back a charge that never touched operating income in the first place.
Taking the Income Statement figure at face value when part of the charge is embedded elsewhere.
Applying an add-back to the target but not consistently across the peer set.

items.q: What’s the logic behind Deferred Tax Liabilities and Deferred Tax Assets?
items.a: In an acquisition, a seller's existing deferred tax assets and liabilities are typically written down to reset their tax basis. New deferred tax liabilities are created when assets are written up, because the incremental book depreciation is not tax-deductible, leading to higher future cash taxes. Conversely, asset write-downs can lead to the creation of new deferred tax assets.
rubric: In an acquisition, a seller's existing deferred tax assets and liabilities are typically written down to reset their tax basis.
New deferred tax liabilities are created when assets are written up, because the incremental book depreciation is not tax-deductible, leading to higher future cash taxes.
Conversely, asset write-downs can lead to the creation of new deferred tax assets.
mistakes: Creating a Deferred Tax Asset from an asset write-up rather than a Liability.
Carrying the seller's existing deferred tax balances through unchanged.
Forgetting that the DTL unwinds as the written-up assets are depreciated.
Applying this treatment to an asset purchase, where the tax basis is stepped up and no DTL arises.

items.q: Let's say that a company sells a subsidiary for $1000, paid for by the buyer in Cash. The buyer is acquiring $500 of Assets with the deal, but it's assuming no Liabilities. Assume a 40% tax rate. What happens on the 3 statements after the sale?
items.a: On the Income Statement, a pre-tax gain of $500 is recorded, increasing Net Income by $300 after a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income increases by $300, the $500 gain is subtracted in Cash Flow from Operations, and the $1,000 sale proceeds are added in Cash Flow from Investing, resulting in a net cash increase of $800. On the Balance Sheet, Cash increases by $800, Assets decrease by $500 (net asset change of +$300), and Shareholders' Equity increases by $300 due to the Net Income boost.
rubric: Records a pre-tax gain of $500, being $1,000 of proceeds against $500 of assets sold.
States that Net Income rises $300 at the 40% tax rate.
Subtracts the $500 non-cash gain within Cash Flow from Operations.
Adds the full $1,000 of proceeds within Cash Flow from Investing.
Arrives at a net cash increase of $800.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Cash up $800 and other Assets down $500 for a net $300, against Shareholders' Equity up $300.
mistakes: Adding the $1,000 of proceeds without reversing the $500 gain, double-counting it.
Increasing cash by the full $1,000 and forgetting the $200 of cash tax on the gain.
Failing to remove the $500 of assets that left with the subsidiary.
Recording a liability adjustment when the buyer assumed none.

items.q: Now let's say that we decide to buy 100% of another company's subsidiary for $1000 in cash. This subsidiary has $500 in Assets and $300 in Liabilities, and we are acquiring all the Assets and assuming all the Liabilities. What happens on the statements immediately afterward?
items.a: On the Income Statement, there are no immediate changes. On the Cash Flow Statement, Cash Flow from Investing decreases by $1,000 due to the acquisition, reducing cash by $1,000. On the Balance Sheet, Cash decreases by $1,000, but you add $500 of the subsidiary's Assets and create $800 of Goodwill (since the purchase price of $1,000 exceeds the net assets of $200), resulting in a net Asset increase of $300; this is balanced by the $300 of assumed Liabilities.
rubric: States that there are no immediate changes to the Income Statement.
Records the $1,000 acquisition as an outflow within Cash Flow from Investing.
Calculates the subsidiary's net assets as $200, being $500 of Assets less $300 of Liabilities.
Creates $800 of Goodwill, the $1,000 price less the $200 of net assets acquired.
Builds the Assets side: Cash down $1,000, the subsidiary's $500 of Assets added, plus $800 of Goodwill, for a net increase of $300.
Balances that against the $300 of assumed Liabilities.
mistakes: Calculating goodwill against the subsidiary's $500 of gross assets rather than its $200 of net assets.
Forgetting to assume the $300 of liabilities, which leaves the Balance Sheet out by that amount.
Recording the acquisition as an expense on the Income Statement.
Classifying the cash outflow under financing rather than investing activities.

items.q: Normally we create Goodwill because we pay more for a company than what its Shareholders’ Equity says it’s worth. But what if the opposite happens? What if we paid $1000 in Cash for a company, but its Assets were worth $2000 and its Liabilities were worth $800?
items.a: If you pay less than the net value of the target's assets, you first attempt to reverse any asset write-ups to see if that resolves the discrepancy. If that is not possible, you must record a "Gain on Bargain Purchase" (Negative Goodwill) on the Income Statement, which increases Net Income. On the Cash Flow Statement, you add back Net Income but subtract the non-cash gain, adjusting cash down by the acquisition cost. On the Balance Sheet, cash decreases by the purchase price, assets increase by the acquired assets' value, and liabilities and equity increase to keep the sheet balanced.
rubric: If you pay less than the net value of the target's assets, you first attempt to reverse any asset write-ups to see if that resolves the discrepancy.
If that is not possible, you must record a "Gain on Bargain Purchase" (Negative Goodwill) on the Income Statement, which increases Net Income.
On the Cash Flow Statement, you add back Net Income but subtract the non-cash gain, adjusting cash down by the acquisition cost.
On the Balance Sheet, cash decreases by the purchase price, assets increase by the acquired assets' value, and liabilities and equity increase to keep the sheet balanced.
mistakes: Recording negative goodwill as an asset or a contra-asset on the Balance Sheet.
Skipping the first step of reassessing the asset write-ups before recognising a gain.
Forgetting to reverse the non-cash gain on the Cash Flow Statement.
Assuming goodwill can be negative - it cannot, which is why the residual runs through the Income Statement.

items.q: Can you explain how the Balance Sheet is adjusted in an LBO model?
items.a: On the Liabilities & Equity side, existing equity is wiped out and replaced by the PE firm's equity contribution, and new debt tranches are added. On the Assets side, cash is adjusted for transaction-related uses, and Goodwill & Other Intangibles are created as a plug to balance the sheet. Other adjustments include asset write-ups, deferred tax liabilities, and capitalized financing fees.
rubric: On the Liabilities & Equity side, existing equity is wiped out and replaced by the PE firm's equity contribution, and new debt tranches are added.
On the Assets side, cash is adjusted for transaction-related uses, and Goodwill & Other Intangibles are created as a plug to balance the sheet.
Other adjustments include asset write-ups, deferred tax liabilities, and capitalized financing fees.
mistakes: Carrying the target's existing equity onto the post-deal balance sheet.
Forgetting the deferred tax liability created by asset write-ups.
Expensing financing fees rather than capitalising them as an asset.
Calculating goodwill without first allocating value to identifiable intangibles.

items.q: Why are Goodwill & Other Intangibles created in an LBO?
items.a: Goodwill and other intangibles represent the premium paid over the book value of the target company's Shareholders' Equity. They act as an accounting plug on the Assets side to balance the newly created Liabilities and Equity, ensuring the balance sheet remains in equilibrium after the acquisition.
rubric: Goodwill and other intangibles represent the premium paid over the book value of the target company's Shareholders' Equity.
They act as an accounting plug on the Assets side to balance the newly created Liabilities and Equity, ensuring the balance sheet remains in equilibrium after the acquisition.
mistakes: Calculating the premium against total assets rather than book equity.
Describing goodwill as a purely arbitrary figure with no economic content.
Forgetting that identifiable intangibles are allocated before the residual becomes goodwill.

items.q: Wait a second, why are Capitalized Financing Fees an Asset?
items.a: Capitalized financing fees are treated as an asset because they represent an upfront cash payment for a service that provides future economic benefits. Similar to prepaid expenses, this asset is amortized over the life of the debt, reducing the company's taxable income in future periods. Since the cash has already been paid, the future amortization represents tax savings without any additional cash outflows.

mistakes: Expensing the financing fee at close, which is the treatment for advisory fees.
Forgetting that the amortisation reduces future taxable income.
Missing the analogy to prepaid expenses, which is what makes it an asset.

items.q: Let's walk through a real-life example of debt modeling now... let's say that we have $100 million of debt with 5% cash interest, 5% PIK interest, and amortization of 10% per year. How do you reflect this on the financial statements?
items.a: On the Income Statement, the $5 million cash interest and $5 million PIK interest combine for a $10 million interest expense, reducing Net Income by $6 million at a 40% tax rate. On the Cash Flow Statement, Net Income is down $6 million, but the $5 million non-cash PIK interest is added back, and the $10 million principal repayment is subtracted under financing activities, resulting in an $11 million net cash decrease. On the Balance Sheet, Cash decreases by $11 million, Debt decreases by a net of $5 million (up $5 million from PIK, down $10 million from repayment), and Shareholders' Equity decreases by $6 million, keeping the sheet balanced.
rubric: Calculates $5 million of cash interest and $5 million of PIK interest for a $10 million total interest expense.
States that Net Income falls $6 million at the 40% tax rate.
Adds back the $5 million of PIK interest on the Cash Flow Statement as a non-cash charge.
Subtracts the $10 million principal repayment under financing activities.
Arrives at a net cash decrease of $11 million.
States that Debt falls a net $5 million: up $5 million from the accrued PIK, down $10 million from the amortisation payment.
Balances the Balance Sheet: Cash down $11 million against Debt down $5 million and Shareholders' Equity down $6 million.
mistakes: Treating PIK interest as a cash payment, overstating the cash outflow by $5 million.
Adding PIK interest to the debt balance but forgetting to add it back on the Cash Flow Statement, or the reverse.
Omitting PIK interest from the Income Statement because no cash moves - it is still an expense.
Netting the PIK accrual against the amortisation and forgetting one of the two.

items.q: Wait a minute - why do we show PIK interest in the Cash Flow from Operations section? Isn't it a financing activity?
items.a: Interest expense is an Income Statement item because it is tax-deductible, so reflecting it in the Cash Flow from Financing section would result in double-counting. PIK interest is shown in the Cash Flow from Operations section because it is a non-cash expense, similar to depreciation. It reduces the company's taxes on the Income Statement but does not actually consume cash, requiring it to be added back to Net Income.

mistakes: Moving PIK interest into the financing section, which double-counts it against Net Income.
Treating PIK as a financing activity because it increases the debt balance.
Forgetting that PIK is tax-deductible despite being non-cash.

items.q: Was ist Leasing?
items.a: Beim Leasing wird dem Leasingnehmer ein zeitlich begrenztes Nutzungsrecht an einem Leasinggegenstand entgeltlich vom Leasinggeber eingeräumt. Je nach Ausgestaltung des Leasingvertrages ähnelt dieser einem Mietverhältnis oder einem verdeckten Kauf.
rubric: Beim Leasing wird dem Leasingnehmer ein zeitlich begrenztes Nutzungsrecht an einem Leasinggegenstand entgeltlich vom Leasinggeber eingeräumt.
Je nach Ausgestaltung des Leasingvertrages ähnelt dieser einem Mietverhältnis oder einem verdeckten Kauf.
mistakes: Leasing mit einem Mietvertrag gleichzusetzen, ohne die Möglichkeit des verdeckten Kaufs zu erwähnen.
Das Nutzungsrecht als Eigentumsübergang zu beschreiben.
Die Entgeltlichkeit zu vergessen, die das Leasing von einer Leihe unterscheidet.

items.q: Welche Vermögensgegenstände sind unter IFRS 16 als Leasinggegenstände zu berücksichtigen?
items.a: Zu den klassischen Leasingobjekten gehören Maschinen, Immobilien, Betriebs- und Geschäftsausstattung sowie Software. Ausgenommen vom Anwendungsbereich des IFRS 16 sind kurzfristige Verträge unter zwölf Monaten, Verträge über geringwertige Wirtschaftsgüter (Schwellenwert von der IASB beispielhaft mit rund 5.000 US-Dollar im Neuzustand angegeben), Lizenzen für Filme oder Urheberrechte, Verträge zur Exploration von Bodenschätzen sowie biologische Vermögenswerte im Anwendungsbereich von IAS 41.
rubric: Nennt klassische Leasingobjekte: Maschinen, Immobilien, Betriebs- und Geschäftsausstattung sowie Software.
Nennt die Ausnahme kurzfristiger Verträge mit einer Laufzeit unter zwölf Monaten.
Nennt die Ausnahme geringwertiger Wirtschaftsgüter und gibt den vom IASB beispielhaft genannten Schwellenwert von rund 5.000 US-Dollar im Neuzustand an.
Nennt die Ausnahme für Lizenzen für Filme und Urheberrechte.
Nennt die Ausnahme für Verträge zur Exploration von Bodenschätzen.
Nennt die Ausnahme für biologische Vermögenswerte im Anwendungsbereich von IAS 41.
mistakes: Biologische Vermögenswerte als Leasinggegenstände nach IFRS 16 einzuordnen - sie sind ausdrücklich ausgenommen und fallen unter IAS 41.
Den Schwellenwert für geringwertige Wirtschaftsgüter in Euro statt in US-Dollar anzugeben.
Den Schwellenwert als feste Regel des Standards zu behandeln, obwohl er lediglich ein Beispiel der IASB in den Basis for Conclusions ist.
Die Zwölf-Monats-Ausnahme zu vergessen, die in der Praxis die häufigste ist.

items.q: Welche zwei Arten des Leasing gibt es beim Leasinggeber?
items.a: Beim Leasinggeber wird zwischen dem Finanzierungsleasing und dem operativen Leasing unterschieden. Die Einstufung hängt davon ab, ob im Wesentlichen alle Chancen und Risiken, die mit dem Eigentum am Leasinggegenstand verbunden sind, auf den Leasingnehmer übertragen werden.
rubric: Beim Leasinggeber wird zwischen dem Finanzierungsleasing und dem operativen Leasing unterschieden.
Die Einstufung hängt davon ab, ob im Wesentlichen alle Chancen und Risiken, die mit dem Eigentum am Leasinggegenstand verbunden sind, auf den Leasingnehmer übertragen werden.
mistakes: Die Unterscheidung an der Vertragslaufzeit statt an der Übertragung von Chancen und Risiken festzumachen.
Die Sicht des Leasinggebers mit der des Leasingnehmers zu verwechseln - nach IFRS 16 entfällt die Unterscheidung nur beim Leasingnehmer.
Finanzierungsleasing und operatives Leasing zu vertauschen.

items.q: Wann und wie wird ein Finanzierungsleasing bilanziert?
items.a: Ein Finanzierungsleasing liegt vor, wenn alle wesentlichen Chancen und Risiken des Eigentums auf den Leasingnehmer übertragen werden. Der Leasinggeber bucht den Vermögenswert aus, erfasst eine Leasingforderung in Höhe des Barwerts der zukünftigen Zahlungen und verbucht die erhaltenen Raten periodengerecht als Zinsertrag.
rubric: Ein Finanzierungsleasing liegt vor, wenn alle wesentlichen Chancen und Risiken des Eigentums auf den Leasingnehmer übertragen werden.
Der Leasinggeber bucht den Vermögenswert aus, erfasst eine Leasingforderung in Höhe des Barwerts der zukünftigen Zahlungen und verbucht die erhaltenen Raten periodengerecht als Zinsertrag.
mistakes: Den Vermögenswert beim Leasinggeber in der Bilanz zu belassen.
Die Leasingforderung zum Nominalwert statt zum Barwert der künftigen Zahlungen anzusetzen.
Die vereinnahmten Raten vollständig als Ertrag zu erfassen, statt sie in Tilgungs- und Zinsanteil aufzuteilen.

items.q: Welchen Vor-, bzw. Nachteil bietet ein Leasingvertrag gegenüber einer Anschaffung?
items.a: Ein Leasingvertrag bietet dem Unternehmen im Vergleich zum direkten Kauf eine deutlich höhere Flexibilität. Demgegenüber stehen jedoch in der Regel höhere langfristige Gesamtkosten für die Nutzung des Objekts.
rubric: Ein Leasingvertrag bietet dem Unternehmen im Vergleich zum direkten Kauf eine deutlich höhere Flexibilität.
Demgegenüber stehen jedoch in der Regel höhere langfristige Gesamtkosten für die Nutzung des Objekts.
mistakes: Nur einen der beiden Aspekte zu nennen, obwohl nach Vor- und Nachteil gefragt ist.
Leasing pauschal als günstiger darzustellen, obwohl die Gesamtkosten über die Laufzeit regelmäßig höher sind.
Die Bilanzwirkung zu ignorieren - seit IFRS 16 steht auch das Leasing beim Leasingnehmer in der Bilanz.
